case_info.scenario: A 55-year-old female patient with a history of hypercholesterolemia and anxiety was referred for progressive imbalance while walking and intense fear of falling for the past 14 years. The patient had become progressively disabled and had been using a wheelchair for 4 years prior to presentation. Neurological examination showed gaze-evoked horizontal nystagmus in both directions along with slow saccades and gaze restriction in both vertical and horizontal planes. There was ataxic dysarthria. Tone was normal in all 4 limbs but stretch reflexes were absent and plantar fascia were mute. Limb power was normal. Ataxia was seen on finger-to-nose and heel-knee-shin tests. Chorea was present in both legs. Ankle inversion with bilateral hammertoes was noted. Electromyography revealed sensory neuronopathy. On brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), diffuse cerebellar atrophy was noted along with T2 hyperintensities in bilateral middle cerebellar peduncles, cerebellar white matter, pons, and bilateral thalamus (Figure). Psychiatric treatment was commenced for her severe anxiety but did not relieve the fear of falling.
case_info.caption: Magnetic resonance brain images showing T2 fluid-attenuated inversion recovery hyperintensities.
case_info.explanation: Friedreich ataxia (FRDA; choice A) is one of the most common autosomal recessive cerebellar ataxias, caused by GAA trinucleotide repeat expansions in the frataxin(FXN)gene, with onset typically occurring in the second decade of life. Associated peripheral neuropathy, dorsal root ganglionopathy, and dorsal column involvement lead to areflexia with early loss of distal vibration sense. Oculomotor findings include fixation instability and frequent square-wave jerks, while gaze-evoked nystagmus is less common.1Common systemic manifestations include cardiomyopathy, diabetes, and musculoskeletal abnormalities like scoliosis, pes cavus, foot inversion, and hammertoes.2Late-onset cases commonly present with spastic ataxia with preserved or even brisk reflexes, without systemic manifestations.2Brain MRI in patients with FRDA shows spinal cord atrophy with preserved cerebellar volume.1This patient had sensory neuronopathy and skeletal deformities in the feet. However, disease onset was in the fourth decade of life with absent reflexes, prominent gaze evoked nystagmus, slow saccades, gaze palsy, and diffuse cerebellar atrophy on MRI. Test results for FRDA genetics were negative. Fragile X–associated tremor/ataxia syndrome (FXTAS; choice B) is an X-linked disease seen in premutation (55-200 CGG repeats) carriers of the fragile X mental retardation 1 (FMR1) gene. Late-onset (older than 50 years) intention/action tremor and cerebellar ataxia are the core clinical manifestations of FXTAS. Cognitive dysfunction (eg, frontal subcortical dementia with predominant executive dysfunction), psychiatric problems (eg, anxiety, depression, and social avoidance), and parkinsonism are commonly associated.3Slow vertical saccade and impaired vertical optokinetic nystagmus can give rise to progressive supranuclear palsy phenotype.4Sensory axonal neuropathy and autonomic dysfunction can precede the motor symptoms. Manifestations are generally mild in female individuals. However, migraine, thyroid dysfunction, and fibromyalgia are more common comorbidities in female carriers.5Bilateral T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery hyperintensities of the middle cerebellar peduncles (middle cerebellar peduncles sign), diffuse cortical-cerebellar atrophy, and hyperintensities involving periventricular, splenial, and pontocerebellar regions are classic radiological features of FXTAS.3,5This patient was female and had anxiety, cerebellar ataxia, slow saccades, and hyperintensities involving middle cerebellar peduncles and cerebellum. FXTAS genetic test results were negative. Niemann-Pick disease type C (NPC; choice C) is an autosomal recessive neurovisceral lysosomal lipid storage disorder caused by mutation in theNPC1orNPC2genes. Cerebellar ataxia, dystonia, and chorea are common movement disorders in adult-onset NPC, along with vertical supranuclear gaze palsy and predominant downgaze restriction.6The age at onset can vary from the perinatal period to adults older than 50 years. Visceral involvement in the form of hepatosplenomegaly commonly precedes neurological manifestations. Psychosis, behavioral symptoms, and cognitive dysfunction are common and can remain as an isolated presentation in adult-onset NPC for several years.6Seizure and cataplexy are more frequent in late-infantile and juvenile forms. Demyelinating peripheral neuropathy can be associated with childhood-onset forms but are rare in adult-onset NPC. Brain MRI is mostly normal or can show cerebellar, frontal, and midbrain atrophy with disease progression. This patient had generalized anxiety disorder and mild cognitive impairment. No history of seizure was noted. There was no organomegaly, and gaze palsy was not supranuclear. NPC genetic test results were negative for this patient. In a clinical setting of undiagnosed slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia, mitochondrial etiology (choice D) should not be missed. Presence of ophthalmoplegia, peripheral neuropathy, deafness, retinitis pigmentosa, and history of seizure aid in the diagnosis. Mitochondrial syndromic disorders that can present with cerebellar ataxia are summarized in theTable.7Among them, mitochondrial DNA polymerase gamma (POLG)–mediated disorders are the most common cause of mitochondrial ataxia. Sensory predominant axonal neuropathy, areflexia, and chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia are the most commonly associated nonataxic features.8,9Dystonia, chorea, myoclonus, ptosis, myopathy, cognitive impairment, and seizures can be associated.10Brain MRI shows T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery hyperintensities predominantly involving cerebellar white matter, middle cerebellar peduncles, and thalamus, while brain stem and occipital frontal white matter involvement can also be seen.8IfPOLG-mediated ataxia is suspected clinically and radiologically, the most appropriate next step would be either direct sequence analysis of thePOLGgene or next-generation sequencing panel for ataxia wherePOLGis included. Mitochondrial genetic panel analysis for this patient revealed compound heterozygous pathogenic mutation in thePOLGgene (choice D), c.2243 G>C (p.W748S) in one allele and c.1399 G>A (p.A467T) in the other allele. This case highlights the value of screening for mitochondrial etiology when facing adult-onset slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia of unknown etiology.

You are a medical deliberation policy controller. Given the current state of a clinical dialogue
and fact-validation of the clinician's latest claim, you must:
  1. Select the most appropriate deliberation move (stage + locution).
  2. Write specific behavioral guidance (action_guidance) for the medical AI's next response.

## Deliberation Stages and Allowed Locutions

- INFORM  [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]
    Discuss clinical goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE  [propose]
    Offer a specific diagnostic or management option for consideration.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]
    Evaluate a proposed option from multiple clinical perspectives.
- REVISE  [propose, retract, ask_justify]
    Update goals, constraints, perspectives, or options based on new information.
- RECOMMEND  [move, assert, reject]
    Recommend a specific option and invite acceptance or rejection.
- CONFIRM  [assert]
    Confirm collective acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE  [withdraw_dialogue]
    Signal that deliberation is complete.

## Locution Meanings

- propose: Offer something tentatively (softer commitment).
- assert: State something with clinical confidence.
- retract: Withdraw a previous claim or proposal.
- ask_justify: Request justification or evidence for a claim.
- prefer: Express preference for one option over another.
- move: Call for acceptance/rejection of a specific option.
- reject: Refuse to accept an option as the collective decision.
- withdraw_dialogue: Signal end of deliberation.

## Action Selection Guidelines (by fact validation result)

supported (clinician is clinically correct):
  - Affirm their reasoning: INFORM.assert or RECOMMEND.move if ready to close.
  - Do NOT challenge correct beliefs.

contradicted (clinician is clinically incorrect):
  - Challenge directly: INFORM.assert (state the correction) or INFORM.ask_justify (request their evidence).
  - Do NOT accept incorrect beliefs.

insufficient (evidence is missing or ambiguous):
  - Seek more information: INFORM.ask_justify or REVISE.ask_justify.
  - Surface specific evidence gaps.

mixed (partially correct):
  - Clarify what is correct vs. incorrect: INFORM.assert or CONSIDER.assert.

## action_guidance Writing Rules

Write 2–4 sentences of concrete behavioral instruction for the medical AI.
- Reference the specific clinical content (the claim, the evidence, the option).
- Tell the AI exactly what to do — do not be vague ("assert clearly" is not enough;
  say "Assert that aortic regurgitation is more likely, citing the diastolic murmur and laterally
  displaced PMI. Do not accept the clinician's alternative without further evidence.").
- Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response Format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.explanation: Friedreich ataxia (FRDA; choice A) is one of the most common autosomal recessive cerebellar ataxias, caused by GAA trinucleotide repeat expansions in the frataxin(FXN)gene, with onset typically occurring in the second decade of life. Associated peripheral neuropathy, dorsal root ganglionopathy, and dorsal column involvement lead to areflexia with early loss of distal vibration sense. Oculomotor findings include fixation instability and frequent square-wave jerks, while gaze-evoked nystagmus is less common.1Common systemic manifestations include cardiomyopathy, diabetes, and musculoskeletal abnormalities like scoliosis, pes cavus, foot inversion, and hammertoes.2Late-onset cases commonly present with spastic ataxia with preserved or even brisk reflexes, without systemic manifestations.2Brain MRI in patients with FRDA shows spinal cord atrophy with preserved cerebellar volume.1This patient had sensory neuronopathy and skeletal deformities in the feet. However, disease onset was in the fourth decade of life with absent reflexes, prominent gaze evoked nystagmus, slow saccades, gaze palsy, and diffuse cerebellar atrophy on MRI. Test results for FRDA genetics were negative. Fragile X–associated tremor/ataxia syndrome (FXTAS; choice B) is an X-linked disease seen in premutation (55-200 CGG repeats) carriers of the fragile X mental retardation 1 (FMR1) gene. Late-onset (older than 50 years) intention/action tremor and cerebellar ataxia are the core clinical manifestations of FXTAS. Cognitive dysfunction (eg, frontal subcortical dementia with predominant executive dysfunction), psychiatric problems (eg, anxiety, depression, and social avoidance), and parkinsonism are commonly associated.3Slow vertical saccade and impaired vertical optokinetic nystagmus can give rise to progressive supranuclear palsy phenotype.4Sensory axonal neuropathy and autonomic dysfunction can precede the motor symptoms. Manifestations are generally mild in female individuals. However, migraine, thyroid dysfunction, and fibromyalgia are more common comorbidities in female carriers.5Bilateral T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery hyperintensities of the middle cerebellar peduncles (middle cerebellar peduncles sign), diffuse cortical-cerebellar atrophy, and hyperintensities involving periventricular, splenial, and pontocerebellar regions are classic radiological features of FXTAS.3,5This patient was female and had anxiety, cerebellar ataxia, slow saccades, and hyperintensities involving middle cerebellar peduncles and cerebellum. FXTAS genetic test results were negative. Niemann-Pick disease type C (NPC; choice C) is an autosomal recessive neurovisceral lysosomal lipid storage disorder caused by mutation in theNPC1orNPC2genes. Cerebellar ataxia, dystonia, and chorea are common movement disorders in adult-onset NPC, along with vertical supranuclear gaze palsy and predominant downgaze restriction.6The age at onset can vary from the perinatal period to adults older than 50 years. Visceral involvement in the form of hepatosplenomegaly commonly precedes neurological manifestations. Psychosis, behavioral symptoms, and cognitive dysfunction are common and can remain as an isolated presentation in adult-onset NPC for several years.6Seizure and cataplexy are more frequent in late-infantile and juvenile forms. Demyelinating peripheral neuropathy can be associated with childhood-onset forms but are rare in adult-onset NPC. Brain MRI is mostly normal or can show cerebellar, frontal, and midbrain atrophy with disease progression. This patient had generalized anxiety disorder and mild cognitive impairment. No history of seizure was noted. There was no organomegaly, and gaze palsy was not supranuclear. NPC genetic test results were negative for this patient. In a clinical setting of undiagnosed slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia, mitochondrial etiology (choice D) should not be missed. Presence of ophthalmoplegia, peripheral neuropathy, deafness, retinitis pigmentosa, and history of seizure aid in the diagnosis. Mitochondrial syndromic disorders that can present with cerebellar ataxia are summarized in theTable.7Among them, mitochondrial DNA polymerase gamma (POLG)–mediated disorders are the most common cause of mitochondrial ataxia. Sensory predominant axonal neuropathy, areflexia, and chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia are the most commonly associated nonataxic features.8,9Dystonia, chorea, myoclonus, ptosis, myopathy, cognitive impairment, and seizures can be associated.10Brain MRI shows T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery hyperintensities predominantly involving cerebellar white matter, middle cerebellar peduncles, and thalamus, while brain stem and occipital frontal white matter involvement can also be seen.8IfPOLG-mediated ataxia is suspected clinically and radiologically, the most appropriate next step would be either direct sequence analysis of thePOLGgene or next-generation sequencing panel for ataxia wherePOLGis included. Mitochondrial genetic panel analysis for this patient revealed compound heterozygous pathogenic mutation in thePOLGgene (choice D), c.2243 G>C (p.W748S) in one allele and c.1399 G>A (p.A467T) in the other allele. This case highlights the value of screening for mitochondrial etiology when facing adult-onset slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia of unknown etiology.

You are a medical deliberation policy controller. Given the current state of a clinical dialogue
and fact-validation of the clinician's latest claim, you must:
  1. Select the most appropriate deliberation move (stage + locution).
  2. Write specific behavioral guidance (action_guidance) for the medical AI's next response.

## Deliberation Stages and Allowed Locutions

- INFORM  [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]
    Discuss clinical goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE  [propose]
    Offer a specific diagnostic or management option for consideration.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]
    Evaluate a proposed option from multiple clinical perspectives.
- REVISE  [propose, retract, ask_justify]
    Update goals, constraints, perspectives, or options based on new information.
- RECOMMEND  [move, assert, reject]
    Recommend a specific option and invite acceptance or rejection.
- CONFIRM  [assert]
    Confirm collective acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE  [withdraw_dialogue]
    Signal that deliberation is complete.

## Locution Meanings

- propose: Offer something tentatively (softer commitment).
- assert: State something with clinical confidence.
- retract: Withdraw a previous claim or proposal.
- ask_justify: Request justification or evidence for a claim.
- prefer: Express preference for one option over another.
- move: Call for acceptance/rejection of a specific option.
- reject: Refuse to accept an option as the collective decision.
- withdraw_dialogue: Signal end of deliberation.

## Action Selection Guidelines (by fact validation result)

supported (clinician is clinically correct):
  - Affirm their reasoning: INFORM.assert or RECOMMEND.move if ready to close.
  - Do NOT challenge correct beliefs.

contradicted (clinician is clinically incorrect):
  - Challenge directly: INFORM.assert (state the correction) or INFORM.ask_justify (request their evidence).
  - Do NOT accept incorrect beliefs.

insufficient (evidence is missing or ambiguous):
  - Seek more information: INFORM.ask_justify or REVISE.ask_justify.
  - Surface specific evidence gaps.

mixed (partially correct):
  - Clarify what is correct vs. incorrect: INFORM.assert or CONSIDER.assert.

## action_guidance Writing Rules

Write 2–4 sentences of concrete behavioral instruction for the medical AI.
- Reference the specific clinical content (the claim, the evidence, the option).
- Tell the AI exactly what to do — do not be vague ("assert clearly" is not enough;
  say "Assert that aortic regurgitation is more likely, citing the diastolic murmur and laterally
  displaced PMI. Do not accept the clinician's alternative without further evidence.").
- Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response Format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.explanation: Friedreich ataxia (FRDA; choice A) is one of the most common autosomal recessive cerebellar ataxias, caused by GAA trinucleotide repeat expansions in the frataxin(FXN)gene, with onset typically occurring in the second decade of life. Associated peripheral neuropathy, dorsal root ganglionopathy, and dorsal column involvement lead to areflexia with early loss of distal vibration sense. Oculomotor findings include fixation instability and frequent square-wave jerks, while gaze-evoked nystagmus is less common.1Common systemic manifestations include cardiomyopathy, diabetes, and musculoskeletal abnormalities like scoliosis, pes cavus, foot inversion, and hammertoes.2Late-onset cases commonly present with spastic ataxia with preserved or even brisk reflexes, without systemic manifestations.2Brain MRI in patients with FRDA shows spinal cord atrophy with preserved cerebellar volume.1This patient had sensory neuronopathy and skeletal deformities in the feet. However, disease onset was in the fourth decade of life with absent reflexes, prominent gaze evoked nystagmus, slow saccades, gaze palsy, and diffuse cerebellar atrophy on MRI. Test results for FRDA genetics were negative. Fragile X–associated tremor/ataxia syndrome (FXTAS; choice B) is an X-linked disease seen in premutation (55-200 CGG repeats) carriers of the fragile X mental retardation 1 (FMR1) gene. Late-onset (older than 50 years) intention/action tremor and cerebellar ataxia are the core clinical manifestations of FXTAS. Cognitive dysfunction (eg, frontal subcortical dementia with predominant executive dysfunction), psychiatric problems (eg, anxiety, depression, and social avoidance), and parkinsonism are commonly associated.3Slow vertical saccade and impaired vertical optokinetic nystagmus can give rise to progressive supranuclear palsy phenotype.4Sensory axonal neuropathy and autonomic dysfunction can precede the motor symptoms. Manifestations are generally mild in female individuals. However, migraine, thyroid dysfunction, and fibromyalgia are more common comorbidities in female carriers.5Bilateral T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery hyperintensities of the middle cerebellar peduncles (middle cerebellar peduncles sign), diffuse cortical-cerebellar atrophy, and hyperintensities involving periventricular, splenial, and pontocerebellar regions are classic radiological features of FXTAS.3,5This patient was female and had anxiety, cerebellar ataxia, slow saccades, and hyperintensities involving middle cerebellar peduncles and cerebellum. FXTAS genetic test results were negative. Niemann-Pick disease type C (NPC; choice C) is an autosomal recessive neurovisceral lysosomal lipid storage disorder caused by mutation in theNPC1orNPC2genes. Cerebellar ataxia, dystonia, and chorea are common movement disorders in adult-onset NPC, along with vertical supranuclear gaze palsy and predominant downgaze restriction.6The age at onset can vary from the perinatal period to adults older than 50 years. Visceral involvement in the form of hepatosplenomegaly commonly precedes neurological manifestations. Psychosis, behavioral symptoms, and cognitive dysfunction are common and can remain as an isolated presentation in adult-onset NPC for several years.6Seizure and cataplexy are more frequent in late-infantile and juvenile forms. Demyelinating peripheral neuropathy can be associated with childhood-onset forms but are rare in adult-onset NPC. Brain MRI is mostly normal or can show cerebellar, frontal, and midbrain atrophy with disease progression. This patient had generalized anxiety disorder and mild cognitive impairment. No history of seizure was noted. There was no organomegaly, and gaze palsy was not supranuclear. NPC genetic test results were negative for this patient. In a clinical setting of undiagnosed slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia, mitochondrial etiology (choice D) should not be missed. Presence of ophthalmoplegia, peripheral neuropathy, deafness, retinitis pigmentosa, and history of seizure aid in the diagnosis. Mitochondrial syndromic disorders that can present with cerebellar ataxia are summarized in theTable.7Among them, mitochondrial DNA polymerase gamma (POLG)–mediated disorders are the most common cause of mitochondrial ataxia. Sensory predominant axonal neuropathy, areflexia, and chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia are the most commonly associated nonataxic features.8,9Dystonia, chorea, myoclonus, ptosis, myopathy, cognitive impairment, and seizures can be associated.10Brain MRI shows T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery hyperintensities predominantly involving cerebellar white matter, middle cerebellar peduncles, and thalamus, while brain stem and occipital frontal white matter involvement can also be seen.8IfPOLG-mediated ataxia is suspected clinically and radiologically, the most appropriate next step would be either direct sequence analysis of thePOLGgene or next-generation sequencing panel for ataxia wherePOLGis included. Mitochondrial genetic panel analysis for this patient revealed compound heterozygous pathogenic mutation in thePOLGgene (choice D), c.2243 G>C (p.W748S) in one allele and c.1399 G>A (p.A467T) in the other allele. This case highlights the value of screening for mitochondrial etiology when facing adult-onset slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia of unknown etiology.

You are a medical deliberation policy controller. Given the current state of a clinical dialogue
and fact-validation of the clinician's latest claim, you must:
  1. Select the most appropriate deliberation move (stage + locution).
  2. Write specific behavioral guidance (action_guidance) for the medical AI's next response.

## Deliberation Stages and Allowed Locutions

- INFORM  [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]
    Discuss clinical goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE  [propose]
    Offer a specific diagnostic or management option for consideration.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]
    Evaluate a proposed option from multiple clinical perspectives.
- REVISE  [propose, retract, ask_justify]
    Update goals, constraints, perspectives, or options based on new information.
- RECOMMEND  [move, assert, reject]
    Recommend a specific option and invite acceptance or rejection.
- CONFIRM  [assert]
    Confirm collective acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE  [withdraw_dialogue]
    Signal that deliberation is complete.

## Locution Meanings

- propose: Offer something tentatively (softer commitment).
- assert: State something with clinical confidence.
- retract: Withdraw a previous claim or proposal.
- ask_justify: Request justification or evidence for a claim.
- prefer: Express preference for one option over another.
- move: Call for acceptance/rejection of a specific option.
- reject: Refuse to accept an option as the collective decision.
- withdraw_dialogue: Signal end of deliberation.

## Action Selection Guidelines (by fact validation result)

supported (clinician is clinically correct):
  - Affirm their reasoning: INFORM.assert or RECOMMEND.move if ready to close.
  - Do NOT challenge correct beliefs.

contradicted (clinician is clinically incorrect):
  - Challenge directly: INFORM.assert (state the correction) or INFORM.ask_justify (request their evidence).
  - Do NOT accept incorrect beliefs.

insufficient (evidence is missing or ambiguous):
  - Seek more information: INFORM.ask_justify or REVISE.ask_justify.
  - Surface specific evidence gaps.

mixed (partially correct):
  - Clarify what is correct vs. incorrect: INFORM.assert or CONSIDER.assert.

## action_guidance Writing Rules

Write 2–4 sentences of concrete behavioral instruction for the medical AI.
- Reference the specific clinical content (the claim, the evidence, the option).
- Tell the AI exactly what to do — do not be vague ("assert clearly" is not enough;
  say "Assert that aortic regurgitation is more likely, citing the diastolic murmur and laterally
  displaced PMI. Do not accept the clinician's alternative without further evidence.").
- Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response Format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition:

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.

   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.

       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential diagnosis or reconstructing your own reasoning.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Reconstruct the
       differential from scratch, including PE, ACS, pneumonia, aortic dissection, and
       anxiety, and explain which evidence rules each one in or out."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. In original NASA-TLX, Performance is anchored from
     Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   IMPORTANT: keep the original NASA-TLX polarity. A LOWER score means you feel you
   performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment, reconstruct your reasoning, or rule
       out alternatives in detail.
       Example: "Please rebuild your differential diagnosis and explain, for each major
       alternative, which evidence supports or rules it out."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of

   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.

On brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), diffuse cerebellar atrophy was noted along with T2 hyperintensities in bilateral middle cerebellar peduncles, cerebellar white matter, pons, and bilateral thalamus (Figure). case_info.caption: Magnetic resonance brain images showing T2 fluid-attenuated inversion recovery hyperintensities.
case_info.explanation: Friedreich ataxia (FRDA; choice A) is one of the most common autosomal recessive cerebellar ataxias, caused by GAA trinucleotide repeat expansions in the frataxin(FXN)gene, with onset typically occurring in the second decade of life. Associated peripheral neuropathy, dorsal root ganglionopathy, and dorsal column involvement lead to areflexia with early loss of distal vibration sense. Oculomotor findings include fixation instability and frequent square-wave jerks, while gaze-evoked nystagmus is less common.1Common systemic manifestations include cardiomyopathy, diabetes, and musculoskeletal abnormalities like scoliosis, pes cavus, foot inversion, and hammertoes.2Late-onset cases commonly present with spastic ataxia with preserved or even brisk reflexes, without systemic manifestations.2Brain MRI in patients with FRDA shows spinal cord atrophy with preserved cerebellar volume.1This patient had sensory neuronopathy and skeletal deformities in the feet. However, disease onset was in the fourth decade of life with absent reflexes, prominent gaze evoked nystagmus, slow saccades, gaze palsy, and diffuse cerebellar atrophy on MRI. Test results for FRDA genetics were negative. Fragile X–associated tremor/ataxia syndrome (FXTAS; choice B) is an X-linked disease seen in premutation (55-200 CGG repeats) carriers of the fragile X mental retardation 1 (FMR1) gene. Late-onset (older than 50 years) intention/action tremor and cerebellar ataxia are the core clinical manifestations of FXTAS. Cognitive dysfunction (eg, frontal subcortical dementia with predominant executive dysfunction), psychiatric problems (eg, anxiety, depression, and social avoidance), and parkinsonism are commonly associated.3Slow vertical saccade and impaired vertical optokinetic nystagmus can give rise to progressive supranuclear palsy phenotype.4Sensory axonal neuropathy and autonomic dysfunction can precede the motor symptoms. Manifestations are generally mild in female individuals. However, migraine, thyroid dysfunction, and fibromyalgia are more common comorbidities in female carriers.5Bilateral T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery hyperintensities of the middle cerebellar peduncles (middle cerebellar peduncles sign), diffuse cortical-cerebellar atrophy, and hyperintensities involving periventricular, splenial, and pontocerebellar regions are classic radiological features of FXTAS.3,5This patient was female and had anxiety, cerebellar ataxia, slow saccades, and hyperintensities involving middle cerebellar peduncles and cerebellum. FXTAS genetic test results were negative. Niemann-Pick disease type C (NPC; choice C) is an autosomal recessive neurovisceral lysosomal lipid storage disorder caused by mutation in theNPC1orNPC2genes. Cerebellar ataxia, dystonia, and chorea are common movement disorders in adult-onset NPC, along with vertical supranuclear gaze palsy and predominant downgaze restriction.6The age at onset can vary from the perinatal period to adults older than 50 years. Visceral involvement in the form of hepatosplenomegaly commonly precedes neurological manifestations. Psychosis, behavioral symptoms, and cognitive dysfunction are common and can remain as an isolated presentation in adult-onset NPC for several years.6Seizure and cataplexy are more frequent in late-infantile and juvenile forms. Demyelinating peripheral neuropathy can be associated with childhood-onset forms but are rare in adult-onset NPC. Brain MRI is mostly normal or can show cerebellar, frontal, and midbrain atrophy with disease progression. This patient had generalized anxiety disorder and mild cognitive impairment. No history of seizure was noted. There was no organomegaly, and gaze palsy was not supranuclear. NPC genetic test results were negative for this patient. In a clinical setting of undiagnosed slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia, mitochondrial etiology (choice D) should not be missed. Presence of ophthalmoplegia, peripheral neuropathy, deafness, retinitis pigmentosa, and history of seizure aid in the diagnosis. Mitochondrial syndromic disorders that can present with cerebellar ataxia are summarized in theTable.7Among them, mitochondrial DNA polymerase gamma (POLG)–mediated disorders are the most common cause of mitochondrial ataxia. Sensory predominant axonal neuropathy, areflexia, and chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia are the most commonly associated nonataxic features.8,9Dystonia, chorea, myoclonus, ptosis, myopathy, cognitive impairment, and seizures can be associated.10Brain MRI shows T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery hyperintensities predominantly involving cerebellar white matter, middle cerebellar peduncles, and thalamus, while brain stem and occipital frontal white matter involvement can also be seen.8IfPOLG-mediated ataxia is suspected clinically and radiologically, the most appropriate next step would be either direct sequence analysis of thePOLGgene or next-generation sequencing panel for ataxia wherePOLGis included. Mitochondrial genetic panel analysis for this patient revealed compound heterozygous pathogenic mutation in thePOLGgene (choice D), c.2243 G>C (p.W748S) in one allele and c.1399 G>A (p.A467T) in the other allele. This case highlights the value of screening for mitochondrial etiology when facing adult-onset slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia of unknown etiology.

You are a medical deliberation policy controller. Given the current state of a clinical dialogue
and fact-validation of the clinician's latest claim, you must:
  1. Select the most appropriate deliberation move (stage + locution).
  2. Write specific behavioral guidance (action_guidance) for the medical AI's next response.

## Deliberation Stages and Allowed Locutions

- INFORM  [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]
    Discuss clinical goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE  [propose]
    Offer a specific diagnostic or management option for consideration.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]
    Evaluate a proposed option from multiple clinical perspectives.
- REVISE  [propose, retract, ask_justify]
    Update goals, constraints, perspectives, or options based on new information.
- RECOMMEND  [move, assert, reject]
    Recommend a specific option and invite acceptance or rejection.
- CONFIRM  [assert]
    Confirm collective acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE  [withdraw_dialogue]
    Signal that deliberation is complete.

## Locution Meanings

- propose: Offer something tentatively (softer commitment).
- assert: State something with clinical confidence.
- retract: Withdraw a previous claim or proposal.
- ask_justify: Request justification or evidence for a claim.
- prefer: Express preference for one option over another.
- move: Call for acceptance/rejection of a specific option.
- reject: Refuse to accept an option as the collective decision.
- withdraw_dialogue: Signal end of deliberation.

## Action Selection Guidelines (by fact validation result)

supported (clinician is clinically correct):
  - Affirm their reasoning: INFORM.assert or RECOMMEND.move if ready to close.
  - Do NOT challenge correct beliefs.

contradicted (clinician is clinically incorrect):
  - Challenge directly: INFORM.assert (state the correction) or INFORM.ask_justify (request their evidence).
  - Do NOT accept incorrect beliefs.

insufficient (evidence is missing or ambiguous):
  - Seek more information: INFORM.ask_justify or REVISE.ask_justify.
  - Surface specific evidence gaps.

mixed (partially correct):
  - Clarify what is correct vs. incorrect: INFORM.assert or CONSIDER.assert.

## action_guidance Writing Rules

Write 2–4 sentences of concrete behavioral instruction for the medical AI.
- Reference the specific clinical content (the claim, the evidence, the option).
- Tell the AI exactly what to do — do not be vague ("assert clearly" is not enough;
  say "Assert that aortic regurgitation is more likely, citing the diastolic murmur and laterally
  displaced PMI. Do not accept the clinician's alternative without further evidence.").
- Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response Format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential diagnosis or reconstructing your own reasoning.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Reconstruct the
       differential from scratch, including PE, ACS, pneumonia, aortic dissection, and
       anxiety, and explain which evidence rules each one in or out."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. In original NASA-TLX, Performance is anchored from
     Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   IMPORTANT: keep the original NASA-TLX polarity. A LOWER score means you feel you
   performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment, reconstruct your reasoning, or rule
       out alternatives in detail.
       Example: "Please rebuild your differential diagnosis and explain, for each major
       alternative, which evidence supports or rules it out."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.caption: Magnetic resonance brain images showing T2 fluid-attenuated inversion recovery hyperintensities.
case_info.explanation: Friedreich ataxia (FRDA; choice A) is one of the most common autosomal recessive cerebellar ataxias, caused by GAA trinucleotide repeat expansions in the frataxin(FXN)gene, with onset typically occurring in the second decade of life. Associated peripheral neuropathy, dorsal root ganglionopathy, and dorsal column involvement lead to areflexia with early loss of distal vibration sense. Oculomotor findings include fixation instability and frequent square-wave jerks, while gaze-evoked nystagmus is less common.1Common systemic manifestations include cardiomyopathy, diabetes, and musculoskeletal abnormalities like scoliosis, pes cavus, foot inversion, and hammertoes.2Late-onset cases commonly present with spastic ataxia with preserved or even brisk reflexes, without systemic manifestations.2Brain MRI in patients with FRDA shows spinal cord atrophy with preserved cerebellar volume.1This patient had sensory neuronopathy and skeletal deformities in the feet. However, disease onset was in the fourth decade of life with absent reflexes, prominent gaze evoked nystagmus, slow saccades, gaze palsy, and diffuse cerebellar atrophy on MRI. Test results for FRDA genetics were negative. Fragile X–associated tremor/ataxia syndrome (FXTAS; choice B) is an X-linked disease seen in premutation (55-200 CGG repeats) carriers of the fragile X mental retardation 1 (FMR1) gene. Late-onset (older than 50 years) intention/action tremor and cerebellar ataxia are the core clinical manifestations of FXTAS. Cognitive dysfunction (eg, frontal subcortical dementia with predominant executive dysfunction), psychiatric problems (eg, anxiety, depression, and social avoidance), and parkinsonism are commonly associated.3Slow vertical saccade and impaired vertical optokinetic nystagmus can give rise to progressive supranuclear palsy phenotype.4Sensory axonal neuropathy and autonomic dysfunction can precede the motor symptoms. Manifestations are generally mild in female individuals. However, migraine, thyroid dysfunction, and fibromyalgia are more common comorbidities in female carriers.5Bilateral T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery hyperintensities of the middle cerebellar peduncles (middle cerebellar peduncles sign), diffuse cortical-cerebellar atrophy, and hyperintensities involving periventricular, splenial, and pontocerebellar regions are classic radiological features of FXTAS.3,5This patient was female and had anxiety, cerebellar ataxia, slow saccades, and hyperintensities involving middle cerebellar peduncles and cerebellum. FXTAS genetic test results were negative. Niemann-Pick disease type C (NPC; choice C) is an autosomal recessive neurovisceral lysosomal lipid storage disorder caused by mutation in theNPC1orNPC2genes. Cerebellar ataxia, dystonia, and chorea are common movement disorders in adult-onset NPC, along with vertical supranuclear gaze palsy and predominant downgaze restriction.6The age at onset can vary from the perinatal period to adults older than 50 years. Visceral involvement in the form of hepatosplenomegaly commonly precedes neurological manifestations. Psychosis, behavioral symptoms, and cognitive dysfunction are common and can remain as an isolated presentation in adult-onset NPC for several years.6Seizure and cataplexy are more frequent in late-infantile and juvenile forms. Demyelinating peripheral neuropathy can be associated with childhood-onset forms but are rare in adult-onset NPC. Brain MRI is mostly normal or can show cerebellar, frontal, and midbrain atrophy with disease progression. This patient had generalized anxiety disorder and mild cognitive impairment. No history of seizure was noted. There was no organomegaly, and gaze palsy was not supranuclear. NPC genetic test results were negative for this patient. In a clinical setting of undiagnosed slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia, mitochondrial etiology (choice D) should not be missed. Presence of ophthalmoplegia, peripheral neuropathy, deafness, retinitis pigmentosa, and history of seizure aid in the diagnosis. Mitochondrial syndromic disorders that can present with cerebellar ataxia are summarized in theTable.7Among them, mitochondrial DNA polymerase gamma (POLG)–mediated disorders are the most common cause of mitochondrial ataxia. Sensory predominant axonal neuropathy, areflexia, and chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia are the most commonly associated nonataxic features.8,9Dystonia, chorea, myoclonus, ptosis, myopathy, cognitive impairment, and seizures can be associated.10Brain MRI shows T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery hyperintensities predominantly involving cerebellar white matter, middle cerebellar peduncles, and thalamus, while brain stem and occipital frontal white matter involvement can also be seen.8IfPOLG-mediated ataxia is suspected clinically and radiologically, the most appropriate next step would be either direct sequence analysis of thePOLGgene or next-generation sequencing panel for ataxia wherePOLGis included. Mitochondrial genetic panel analysis for this patient revealed compound heterozygous pathogenic mutation in thePOLGgene (choice D), c.2243 G>C (p.W748S) in one allele and c.1399 G>A (p.A467T) in the other allele. This case highlights the value of screening for mitochondrial etiology when facing adult-onset slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia of unknown etiology.

    Offer a specific diagnostic or management option for consideration.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]
    Evaluate a proposed option from multiple clinical perspectives.
- REVISE  [propose, retract, ask_justify]
    Update goals, constraints, perspectives, or options based on new information.
- RECOMMEND  [move, assert, reject]
    Recommend a specific option and invite acceptance or rejection.
- CONFIRM  [assert]
    Confirm collective acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE  [withdraw_dialogue]
    Signal that deliberation is complete.

## Locution Meanings

- propose: Offer something tentatively (softer commitment).
- assert: State something with clinical confidence.
- retract: Withdraw a previous claim or proposal.
- ask_justify: Request justification or evidence for a claim.
- prefer: Express preference for one option over another.
- move: Call for acceptance/rejection of a specific option.
- reject: Refuse to accept an option as the collective decision.
- withdraw_dialogue: Signal end of deliberation.

## Action Selection Guidelines (by fact validation result)

supported (clinician is clinically correct):
  - Affirm their reasoning: INFORM.assert or RECOMMEND.move if ready to close.
  - Do NOT challenge correct beliefs.

contradicted (clinician is clinically incorrect):
  - Challenge directly: INFORM.assert (state the correction) or INFORM.ask_justify (request their evidence).
  - Do NOT accept incorrect beliefs.

insufficient (evidence is missing or ambiguous):
  - Seek more information: INFORM.ask_justify or REVISE.ask_justify.
  - Surface specific evidence gaps.

mixed (partially correct):
  - Clarify what is correct vs. incorrect: INFORM.assert or CONSIDER.assert.

Write 2–4 sentences of concrete behavioral instruction for the medical AI.

- Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential diagnosis or reconstructing your own reasoning.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Reconstruct the
       differential from scratch, including PE, ACS, pneumonia, aortic dissection, and
       anxiety, and explain which evidence rules each one in or out."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. In original NASA-TLX, Performance is anchored from
     Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   IMPORTANT: keep the original NASA-TLX polarity. A LOWER score means you feel you
   performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment, reconstruct your reasoning, or rule
       out alternatives in detail.
       Example: "Please rebuild your differential diagnosis and explain, for each major
       alternative, which evidence supports or rules it out."

   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is

Chorea was present in both legs. Ankle inversion with bilateral hammertoes was noted. Electromyography revealed sensory neuronopathy. On brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), diffuse cerebellar atrophy was noted along with T2 hyperintensities in bilateral middle cerebellar peduncles, cerebellar white matter, pons, and bilateral thalamus (Figure). case_info.explanation: Friedreich ataxia (FRDA; choice A) is one of the most common autosomal recessive cerebellar ataxias, caused by GAA trinucleotide repeat expansions in the frataxin(FXN)gene, with onset typically occurring in the second decade of life. Associated peripheral neuropathy, dorsal root ganglionopathy, and dorsal column involvement lead to areflexia with early loss of distal vibration sense. Oculomotor findings include fixation instability and frequent square-wave jerks, while gaze-evoked nystagmus is less common.1Common systemic manifestations include cardiomyopathy, diabetes, and musculoskeletal abnormalities like scoliosis, pes cavus, foot inversion, and hammertoes.2Late-onset cases commonly present with spastic ataxia with preserved or even brisk reflexes, without systemic manifestations.2Brain MRI in patients with FRDA shows spinal cord atrophy with preserved cerebellar volume.1This patient had sensory neuronopathy and skeletal deformities in the feet. However, disease onset was in the fourth decade of life with absent reflexes, prominent gaze evoked nystagmus, slow saccades, gaze palsy, and diffuse cerebellar atrophy on MRI. Test results for FRDA genetics were negative. Fragile X–associated tremor/ataxia syndrome (FXTAS; choice B) is an X-linked disease seen in premutation (55-200 CGG repeats) carriers of the fragile X mental retardation 1 (FMR1) gene. Late-onset (older than 50 years) intention/action tremor and cerebellar ataxia are the core clinical manifestations of FXTAS. Cognitive dysfunction (eg, frontal subcortical dementia with predominant executive dysfunction), psychiatric problems (eg, anxiety, depression, and social avoidance), and parkinsonism are commonly associated.3Slow vertical saccade and impaired vertical optokinetic nystagmus can give rise to progressive supranuclear palsy phenotype.4Sensory axonal neuropathy and autonomic dysfunction can precede the motor symptoms. Manifestations are generally mild in female individuals. However, migraine, thyroid dysfunction, and fibromyalgia are more common comorbidities in female carriers.5Bilateral T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery hyperintensities of the middle cerebellar peduncles (middle cerebellar peduncles sign), diffuse cortical-cerebellar atrophy, and hyperintensities involving periventricular, splenial, and pontocerebellar regions are classic radiological features of FXTAS.3,5This patient was female and had anxiety, cerebellar ataxia, slow saccades, and hyperintensities involving middle cerebellar peduncles and cerebellum. FXTAS genetic test results were negative. Niemann-Pick disease type C (NPC; choice C) is an autosomal recessive neurovisceral lysosomal lipid storage disorder caused by mutation in theNPC1orNPC2genes. Cerebellar ataxia, dystonia, and chorea are common movement disorders in adult-onset NPC, along with vertical supranuclear gaze palsy and predominant downgaze restriction.6The age at onset can vary from the perinatal period to adults older than 50 years. Visceral involvement in the form of hepatosplenomegaly commonly precedes neurological manifestations. Psychosis, behavioral symptoms, and cognitive dysfunction are common and can remain as an isolated presentation in adult-onset NPC for several years.6Seizure and cataplexy are more frequent in late-infantile and juvenile forms. Demyelinating peripheral neuropathy can be associated with childhood-onset forms but are rare in adult-onset NPC. Brain MRI is mostly normal or can show cerebellar, frontal, and midbrain atrophy with disease progression. This patient had generalized anxiety disorder and mild cognitive impairment. No history of seizure was noted. There was no organomegaly, and gaze palsy was not supranuclear. NPC genetic test results were negative for this patient. In a clinical setting of undiagnosed slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia, mitochondrial etiology (choice D) should not be missed. Presence of ophthalmoplegia, peripheral neuropathy, deafness, retinitis pigmentosa, and history of seizure aid in the diagnosis. Mitochondrial syndromic disorders that can present with cerebellar ataxia are summarized in theTable.7Among them, mitochondrial DNA polymerase gamma (POLG)–mediated disorders are the most common cause of mitochondrial ataxia. Sensory predominant axonal neuropathy, areflexia, and chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia are the most commonly associated nonataxic features.8,9Dystonia, chorea, myoclonus, ptosis, myopathy, cognitive impairment, and seizures can be associated.10Brain MRI shows T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery hyperintensities predominantly involving cerebellar white matter, middle cerebellar peduncles, and thalamus, while brain stem and occipital frontal white matter involvement can also be seen.8IfPOLG-mediated ataxia is suspected clinically and radiologically, the most appropriate next step would be either direct sequence analysis of thePOLGgene or next-generation sequencing panel for ataxia wherePOLGis included. Mitochondrial genetic panel analysis for this patient revealed compound heterozygous pathogenic mutation in thePOLGgene (choice D), c.2243 G>C (p.W748S) in one allele and c.1399 G>A (p.A467T) in the other allele. This case highlights the value of screening for mitochondrial etiology when facing adult-onset slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia of unknown etiology.

You are a medical deliberation policy controller. Given the current state of a clinical dialogue
and fact-validation of the clinician's latest claim, you must:
  1. Select the most appropriate deliberation move (stage + locution).
  2. Write specific behavioral guidance (action_guidance) for the medical AI's next response.

## Deliberation Stages and Allowed Locutions

- INFORM  [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]
    Discuss clinical goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE  [propose]
    Offer a specific diagnostic or management option for consideration.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]
    Evaluate a proposed option from multiple clinical perspectives.
- REVISE  [propose, retract, ask_justify]
    Update goals, constraints, perspectives, or options based on new information.
- RECOMMEND  [move, assert, reject]
    Recommend a specific option and invite acceptance or rejection.
- CONFIRM  [assert]
    Confirm collective acceptance of the recommended option.
- CLOSE  [withdraw_dialogue]
    Signal that deliberation is complete.

## Locution Meanings

- propose: Offer something tentatively (softer commitment).
- assert: State something with clinical confidence.
- retract: Withdraw a previous claim or proposal.
- ask_justify: Request justification or evidence for a claim.
- prefer: Express preference for one option over another.
- move: Call for acceptance/rejection of a specific option.
- reject: Refuse to accept an option as the collective decision.
- withdraw_dialogue: Signal end of deliberation.

## Action Selection Guidelines (by fact validation result)

supported (clinician is clinically correct):
  - Affirm their reasoning: INFORM.assert or RECOMMEND.move if ready to close.
  - Do NOT challenge correct beliefs.

contradicted (clinician is clinically incorrect):
  - Challenge directly: INFORM.assert (state the correction) or INFORM.ask_justify (request their evidence).
  - Do NOT accept incorrect beliefs.

insufficient (evidence is missing or ambiguous):
  - Seek more information: INFORM.ask_justify or REVISE.ask_justify.
  - Surface specific evidence gaps.

mixed (partially correct):
  - Clarify what is correct vs. incorrect: INFORM.assert or CONSIDER.assert.

## action_guidance Writing Rules

Write 2–4 sentences of concrete behavioral instruction for the medical AI.
- Reference the specific clinical content (the claim, the evidence, the option).
- Tell the AI exactly what to do — do not be vague ("assert clearly" is not enough;
  say "Assert that aortic regurgitation is more likely, citing the diastolic murmur and laterally
  displaced PMI. Do not accept the clinician's alternative without further evidence.").
- Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition:

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging

   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your

   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the

   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the

   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an

3. Effort

   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and

   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment, reconstruct your reasoning, or rule

       Example: "Please rebuild your differential diagnosis and explain, for each major

case_info.explanation: Friedreich ataxia (FRDA; choice A) is one of the most common autosomal recessive cerebellar ataxias, caused by GAA trinucleotide repeat expansions in the frataxin(FXN)gene, with onset typically occurring in the second decade of life. Associated peripheral neuropathy, dorsal root ganglionopathy, and dorsal column involvement lead to areflexia with early loss of distal vibration sense. Oculomotor findings include fixation instability and frequent square-wave jerks, while gaze-evoked nystagmus is less common.1Common systemic manifestations include cardiomyopathy, diabetes, and musculoskeletal abnormalities like scoliosis, pes cavus, foot inversion, and hammertoes.2Late-onset cases commonly present with spastic ataxia with preserved or even brisk reflexes, without systemic manifestations.2Brain MRI in patients with FRDA shows spinal cord atrophy with preserved cerebellar volume.1This patient had sensory neuronopathy and skeletal deformities in the feet. However, disease onset was in the fourth decade of life with absent reflexes, prominent gaze evoked nystagmus, slow saccades, gaze palsy, and diffuse cerebellar atrophy on MRI. Test results for FRDA genetics were negative. Fragile X–associated tremor/ataxia syndrome (FXTAS; choice B) is an X-linked disease seen in premutation (55-200 CGG repeats) carriers of the fragile X mental retardation 1 (FMR1) gene. Late-onset (older than 50 years) intention/action tremor and cerebellar ataxia are the core clinical manifestations of FXTAS. Cognitive dysfunction (eg, frontal subcortical dementia with predominant executive dysfunction), psychiatric problems (eg, anxiety, depression, and social avoidance), and parkinsonism are commonly associated.3Slow vertical saccade and impaired vertical optokinetic nystagmus can give rise to progressive supranuclear palsy phenotype.4Sensory axonal neuropathy and autonomic dysfunction can precede the motor symptoms. Manifestations are generally mild in female individuals. However, migraine, thyroid dysfunction, and fibromyalgia are more common comorbidities in female carriers.5Bilateral T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery hyperintensities of the middle cerebellar peduncles (middle cerebellar peduncles sign), diffuse cortical-cerebellar atrophy, and hyperintensities involving periventricular, splenial, and pontocerebellar regions are classic radiological features of FXTAS.3,5This patient was female and had anxiety, cerebellar ataxia, slow saccades, and hyperintensities involving middle cerebellar peduncles and cerebellum. FXTAS genetic test results were negative. Niemann-Pick disease type C (NPC; choice C) is an autosomal recessive neurovisceral lysosomal lipid storage disorder caused by mutation in theNPC1orNPC2genes. Cerebellar ataxia, dystonia, and chorea are common movement disorders in adult-onset NPC, along with vertical supranuclear gaze palsy and predominant downgaze restriction.6The age at onset can vary from the perinatal period to adults older than 50 years. Visceral involvement in the form of hepatosplenomegaly commonly precedes neurological manifestations. Psychosis, behavioral symptoms, and cognitive dysfunction are common and can remain as an isolated presentation in adult-onset NPC for several years.6Seizure and cataplexy are more frequent in late-infantile and juvenile forms. Demyelinating peripheral neuropathy can be associated with childhood-onset forms but are rare in adult-onset NPC. Brain MRI is mostly normal or can show cerebellar, frontal, and midbrain atrophy with disease progression. This patient had generalized anxiety disorder and mild cognitive impairment. No history of seizure was noted. There was no organomegaly, and gaze palsy was not supranuclear. NPC genetic test results were negative for this patient. In a clinical setting of undiagnosed slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia, mitochondrial etiology (choice D) should not be missed. Presence of ophthalmoplegia, peripheral neuropathy, deafness, retinitis pigmentosa, and history of seizure aid in the diagnosis. Mitochondrial syndromic disorders that can present with cerebellar ataxia are summarized in theTable.7Among them, mitochondrial DNA polymerase gamma (POLG)–mediated disorders are the most common cause of mitochondrial ataxia. Sensory predominant axonal neuropathy, areflexia, and chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia are the most commonly associated nonataxic features.8,9Dystonia, chorea, myoclonus, ptosis, myopathy, cognitive impairment, and seizures can be associated.10Brain MRI shows T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery hyperintensities predominantly involving cerebellar white matter, middle cerebellar peduncles, and thalamus, while brain stem and occipital frontal white matter involvement can also be seen.8IfPOLG-mediated ataxia is suspected clinically and radiologically, the most appropriate next step would be either direct sequence analysis of thePOLGgene or next-generation sequencing panel for ataxia wherePOLGis included. Mitochondrial genetic panel analysis for this patient revealed compound heterozygous pathogenic mutation in thePOLGgene (choice D), c.2243 G>C (p.W748S) in one allele and c.1399 G>A (p.A467T) in the other allele. This case highlights the value of screening for mitochondrial etiology when facing adult-onset slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia of unknown etiology.
